cells.tense: You are working at the table where a thing gets finished and handed on.
cells.ask: At the end of this week, tell one person how you arrived at a rule you keep — where it came from, not just what it says.
cells.core:
You work where something gets finished and handed on. Not a museum keeper and not a courier — you carry what you've learned and you adjust it while you carry it. A rule you inherited gets tested before you pass it along, and the ones that survive arrive with your own voice in them. That's why people take them seriously.

The balance holds because you keep adjusting: you can feel when a thing has been said enough, and you stop there instead of saying it a fourth time. Getting something whole enough to let go of takes a steady hand, and the calibrating is the work. Hand one more thing over this week than feels strictly finished, and let the person do what they like with it.
cells.sheetLine: You test what you pass on, and the testing is the gift.

cells.tense: You will hold the line on how this is done, and the tightening has already run ahead of the doing.
cells.ask: Pick one rule you guard hardest and leave it unsaid for one week — no correcting, no explaining — and see what happens to the people and the work itself.
cells.core:
A form is supposed to carry something and stay loose enough to be used. You hand it over, the person holds it a little differently than you do, and that difference is fine — that's what lets it travel. Somewhere ahead is a version where the form finally gets agreed on, though.

So it gets defended harder each time, and practicing it has quietly turned into enforcing it. The windows close one at a time, and from inside you barely feel it. The frame was built to carry something and ends up carrying itself. Let the rule you guard hardest go unspoken for a week. What still stands when you stop holding it was the real part.
cells.sheetLine: You're defending the form instead of letting it do its work.

cells.tense: Nothing came down to you from anyone, and you have been building it all from scratch since.
cells.ask: Write down the way you actually do one thing — messy, ten bullets, one page — and send it to one other person.
cells.core:
This works best as picking up a method that already works and adding your own turn to it — standing on something solid and going further. The pattern underneath the doing is visible when you look for it. Right now each method gets made again by yourself, and it doesn't quite finish, because it doesn't travel past your own hands.

It feels like independence. It is closer to working alone in a place nobody visits. What is missing is not more effort — pushing harder only makes it emptier. What is missing is the pattern underneath how you already work. Write the method out, one page, no polishing, and put it in someone's hands.

cells.tense: What you do has already reached other people, and you keep describing it as your own small routine.
cells.ask: Tell someone the version of one story you usually keep offstage — the part you thought was too small to mention — and let them hear it.
cells.core:
Named out loud, this is a person shaping how others do the thing and adjusting in the open — adding and subtracting as the room changes, with both sides able to see it. That's already happening. People copy the order you do things in, the phrasing, the little corrections.

You call it habit. It has already left your hands, and your account of it hasn't caught up. Something gets finished here and let go, without you claiming any of it. When you say out loud what you're passing on, the grip in your shoulders eases. Tell one story you keep offstage. Let it land wherever it lands.

attempts.check: Unsupported: that the person has a body of knowledge worth passing on, or people already learning from them — the record supports the capacity, not its history or its audience, so every cell locates the transmission in the moment rather than in a past. A reader could reasonably say 'there is no one learning from me'; the asks still stand, since naming a standard or handing over loose notes does not require an audience to have been watching. The ask survives a wrong read because it is a small action a camera can see, not a claim about them. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you are the teacher here' — it flatters the mechanism and the person can only refuse it.
